claim: Absence seizures result from 3 to 5 Hz generalized thalamocortical oscillations that depend on highly regulated inhibitory neurotransmission in the thalamus.
source: Absence seizures result from 3 to 5 Hz generalized thalamocortical oscillations that depend on highly regulated inhibitory neurotransmission in the thalamus.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about absence seizures.

claim: Efficient reuptake of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA is essential, and reuptake failure worsens human seizures.
source: Efficient reuptake of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA is essential, and reuptake failure worsens human seizures.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about GABA reuptake and its clinical implications.

claim: Blocking either GAT1 or GAT3 prolonged oscillations in acute rat brain slices.
source: As expected, we found that blocking either GAT1 or GAT3 prolonged oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: Blocking both GAT1 and GAT3 unexpectedly suppressed oscillations.
source: However, blocking both GATs unexpectedly suppressed oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: A non-linear dependence of T-type calcium channel gating on GABAB receptor activity regulates network oscillations.
source: Integrating experimental observations into single-neuron and network-level computational models shows how a non-linear dependence of T-type calcium channel gating on GABAB receptor activity regulates network oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results integrated with experimental observations.

claim: Only within a narrow range does prolonging GABAB receptor activity promote channel opening and intensify oscillations.
source: Only within a narrow range does prolonging GABAB receptor activity promote channel opening and intensify oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental and computational data showing the relationship between GABAB receptor activity duration and oscillation intensity.

claim: Receptor activity that is either too brief or too protracted fails to sufficiently open T-type channels necessary for sustaining oscillations.
source: Receptor activity that is either too brief or too protracted fails to sufficiently open T-type channels necessary for sustaining oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling and experimental data showing the effects of different GABAB receptor activation durations.

claim: Cortically projecting neurons of the thalamus produce brief bursts of action potentials following membrane hyperpolarization.
source: Following membrane hyperpolarization, such as that produced by synaptic inhibition, cortically projecting neurons of the thalamus [i.e. thalamocortical (TC) neurons] produce brief bursts of action potentials (Llinás and Jahnsen, 1982), a cellular property that maintains both sleep-related and seizure-related oscillations (McCormick and Contreras, 2001; Huguenard and McCormick, 2007; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CaV3.1 T-type calcium channels sustain post-inhibitory rebound bursts in thalamocortical neurons by producing a relatively prolonged calcium-dependent, low-threshold spike.
source: Several studies have shown that CaV3.1 T-type calcium channels (T channels) sustain post-inhibitory rebound bursts in thalamocortical neurons by producing a relatively prolonged calcium-dependent, low-threshold spike (Kim et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2003; Porcello et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: T channels require membrane depolarization to open and hyperpolarization to recover.
source: These channels require membrane depolarization to open and hyperpolarization to recover (Coulter et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Hyperpolarization-dependent recovery involves the removal of T channel inactivation (i.e. de-inactivation).
source: Hyperpolarization-dependent recovery involves the removal of T channel inactivation (i.e. de-inactivation).
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about T channel gating properties.

claim: T channels are largely inactivated at resting membrane potentials, making membrane hyperpolarization necessary for robust rebound bursting.
source: As T channels are largely inactivated at resting membrane potentials, membrane hyperpolarization is necessary for robust rebound bursting (Llinás and Jahnsen, 1982; Coulter et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reticular thalamic neurons serve as the main source of inhibitory, GABAergic input to thalamocortical neurons, especially in rodents.
source: Reticular thalamic (RT) neurons serve as the main source of inhibitory, GABAergic input to thalamocortical neurons, especially in rodents (Shosaku, 1985; Pinault and Deschênes, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thalamocortical neurons express synaptic α1β2γ2 GABAA receptors, and two types of extrasynaptic receptors: GABAA (α4β2δ) and GABAB.
source: Thalamocortical neurons express synaptic α1β2γ2 GABAA receptors, and two types of extrasynaptic receptors: GABAA (α4β2δ) and GABAB (Pirker et al., 2000; Kulik et al., 2002; Jia et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Modulation of synaptic GABAA receptors on TC neurons has little effect on thalamocortical oscillations.
source: Studies have shown that modulation of synaptic GABAA receptors on TC neurons has little effect on thalamocortical oscillations (Sohal et al., 2003; Rovó et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Extrasynaptic receptors have been implicated in thalamocortical seizures, both for GABAA and GABAB receptors.
source: In contrast, extrasynaptic receptors have been implicated in thalamocortical seizures, both for GABAA (Cope et al., 2009) and GABAB (Liu et al., 1992; Vergnes et al., 1997; Bortolato et al., 2010) receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A shift from GABAA receptor-mediated to GABAB receptor-mediated inhibition at the RT-TC synapse transforms oscillations from a 10 Hz, sparse, spindle-like activity to a 3 Hz, hyper-synchronized, seizure-like state.
source: Prior experimental and computational work has demonstrated that a shift from GABAA receptor-mediated to GABAB receptor-mediated inhibition at the RT-TC synapse transforms oscillations from a 10 Hz, sparse, spindle-like activity to a 3 Hz, hyper-synchronized, seizure-like state (von Krosigk et al., 1993; Destexhe et al., 1996; Destexhe, 1998; Blumenfeld and McCormick, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental and computational research.

claim: GABA transporters powerfully control the activation of GABAB receptors.
source: GABA transporters (GATs) powerfully control the activation of GABAB receptors (Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GAT1 and GAT3 represent the primary GABA transporters expressed in the brain and normally recycle GABA from the extrasynaptic space.
source: GAT1 and GAT3 represent the primary GABA transporters expressed in the brain and normally recycle GABA from the extrasynaptic space, thereby regulating GABA spillover from the synapse and the activation of extrasynaptic GABAA and GABAB receptors (Cope et al., 2009; Scanziani, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the thalamus, GAT3 is localized farther away from synapses than GAT1.
source: In the thalamus, the more abundant transporter, GAT3, is localized farther away from synapses than GAT1 (De Biasi et al., 1998; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Specific GAT1 blockade results only in an increase in the amplitude of the GABAB IPSC.
source: Consequently, specific GAT1 blockade results only in an increase in the amplitude of the GABAB IPSC, reflecting increases in GABA concentration near the synapse.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the spatial localization of GAT1 and prior research.

claim: Specific GAT3 blockade results in an increase in both amplitude and decay of the GABAB-mediated inhibitory post-synaptic current.
source: In contrast, specific GAT3 blockade results in an increase in both amplitude and decay of the GABAB-mediated inhibitory post-synaptic current (GABAB IPSC), as GABA is allowed to diffuse far from the synapse where there is an abundance of GABAB receptors (Kulik et al., 2002; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Dual GAT1 and GAT3 blockade results in a roughly 10-fold increase in the decay time constant of the GABAB IPSC, a supralinear effect relative to single GAT1 or GAT3 blockade.
source: On the other hand, dual GAT1 and GAT3 blockade results in a roughly 10-fold increase in the decay time constant of the GABAB IPSC, a supralinear effect relative to the modest increases for single GAT1 (no increase) or GAT3 (1.5-fold) blockade.
evidence: This claim is based on prior experimental findings.

claim: Oscillations last between 2 and 13 s at baseline in the acute rat brain slice model.
source: By detecting evoked bursts, we found that oscillations last between 2 and 13 s at baseline (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The autocorrelogram of binned spike times revealed pronounced secondary peaks at multiples of approximately 500 ms.
source: The autocorrelogram of binned spike times revealed pronounced secondary peaks at multiples of approximately 500 ms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Individual GAT1 blockade increased oscillation duration by 36% relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline, individual GAT1 or GAT3 blockade increased oscillation duration by 36% (n = 8 slices from five animals, p=0.0027; here and in all results, percentages refer to relative change from control conditions)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Individual GAT3 blockade increased oscillation duration by 99% relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline, individual GAT1 or GAT3 blockade increased oscillation duration by 36% (n = 8 slices from five animals, p=0.0027; here and in all results, percentages refer to relative change from control conditions) and 99%, (n = 7 slices from five animals, p=0.0076), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Blocking GAT1 increased the oscillation period by 13% relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline, blocking either GAT1 or GAT3 increased the oscillation period by 13% (n = 8 slices from five animals, p=0.0021)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Blocking GAT3 increased the oscillation period by 32% relative to baseline.
source: Relative to baseline, blocking either GAT1 or GAT3 increased the oscillation period by 13% (n = 8 slices from five animals, p=0.0021) and 32% (n = 7 slices from five animals, p=0.0050), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade decreased oscillation duration by 48%.
source: Following a brief prolongation during the early phases of drug perfusion (see Figure 1C), dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade eventually decreased oscillation duration by 48% (Figure 1D, n = 9 slices from four animals, p=0.026).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade invariably abolished oscillations after 60 min of drug application.
source: For those slices, dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade invariably abolished oscillations (Figure 1F, n = 5 slices from three animals, p=0.0062).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Relative to dynControl responses, LTS and burst probabilities were higher following either dynGAT1-Block or dynGAT3-Block.
source: Relative to dynControl responses, LTS and burst probabilities were higher following either dynGAT1-Block (n = 47 cells, LTS: +26%, p=0.0080, burst: +63%, p=0.0018) or dynGAT3-Block (n = 47 cells, LTS: +39%, p=0.0015, burst: +106%, p=1.7×10−7)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Relative to dynControl responses, LTS and burst probabilities were lower following dynDual-Block.
source: Relative to dynControl responses, LTS and burst probabilities were higher following either dynGAT1-Block (n = 47 cells, LTS: +26%, p=0.0080, burst: +63%, p=0.0018) or dynGAT3-Block (n = 47 cells, LTS: +39%, p=0.0015, burst: +106%, p=1.7×10−7), but lower following dynDual-Block (n = 47 cells, LTS: −88%, p=4.8×10−6, burst: −82%, p=0.030).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Relative to dynControl responses, average burst latency was modestly prolonged following dynGAT1-Block.
source: Relative to dynControl responses, average LTS latency was not significantly different following dynGAT1-Block (n = 32 cells, p=0.97), while average burst latency was modestly prolonged (+4.6%, n = 21 cells, p=0.034).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: dynGAT3-Block IPSCs significantly prolonged both LTS and burst latency.
source: In contrast, dynGAT3-Block IPSCs significantly prolonged both LTS (+53%, n = 32 cells, p=3.7×10−9) and burst latency (+58%, n = 21 cells, p=1.1×10−9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: All well-fitted model neurons were characterized by high T channel densities in the distal dendrite and high A-type potassium channel densities in the soma.
source: All well-fitted neurons were characterized by high T channel densities in the distal dendrite and high A-type potassium channel densities in the soma (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: To reach LTS threshold, the open probability discrepancy curve must reach an inflection point and the inflection point must have a steep slope.
source: To reach LTS threshold, we identified two criteria that must occur in the open probability discrepancy curve: (1) reach an inflection point and (2) the inflection point must have a steep slope.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling analysis.

claim: Prolonging an LTS-producing simGAT3-Block IPSC decreased T channel open probability discrepancy and abolished LTS responses as time constants increased above four-fold.
source: Prolonging an LTS-producing simGAT3-Block IPSC decreased T channel open probability discrepancy and abolished LTS responses as time constants increased above four-fold (Figure 7A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A1.

claim: Shortening a non-LTS-producing simDual-Block IPSC increased T channel open probability discrepancy and produced LTS responses as time constants decreased by 20%.
source: Conversely, shortening a non-LTS-producing simDual-Block IPSC increased T channel open probability discrepancy and produced LTS responses as time constants decreased by 20% (Figure 7A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7A2.

claim: As the amplitude of the simDual-Block waveform increased while fixing the rise and decay time constants, T channel open probability discrepancy nonetheless remained low and robust LTS responses never emerged.
source: In contrast, as the amplitude of the simDual-Block waveform increased while fixing the rise and decay time constants, T channel open probability discrepancy nonetheless remained low and robust LTS responses never emerged (Figure 7B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B2.

claim: Relative to using simControl parameters, oscillation probability increased when using simGAT1-Block or simGAT3-Block parameters in two-cell networks.
source: Relative to using simControl parameters, oscillation probability increased when using simGAT1-Block parameters (+66%, n = 24 networks, p=0.016) or simGAT3-Block parameters (+93%, p=0.048).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results with statistical analysis.

claim: When simDual-Block parameters were applied in the two-cell network, oscillations did not arise.
source: In contrast, when simDual-Block parameters were applied in the network, oscillations did not arise, consistent with the experimental observation that dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade inevitably abolished oscillations (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results.

claim: For TC-heterogeneous networks, relative to using simControl parameters, oscillation probability increased when using either simGAT1-Block or simGAT3-Block parameters, but decreased when using simDual-Block parameters.
source: Indeed, for the set of TC-heterogeneous networks, relative to using simControl parameters, oscillation probability increased when using either simGAT1-Block (+8.2%, n = 24 networks, p=0.049) or simGAT3-Block parameters (+8.5%, p=0.013), but decreased when using simDual-Block parameters (−82%, p=0.0010).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results with statistical analysis.

claim: Including cell heterogeneity in network simulations provides more robust oscillations and more realistically recapitulates experimental oscillation periods.
source: Furthermore, we found that including cell heterogeneity in network simulations provides more robust oscillations and more realistically recapitulates experimental oscillation periods by averaging out LTS response heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results comparing homogeneous and heterogeneous networks.

claim: The GAT1 blocker tiagabine can induce continuous spike-wave discharges in patients with absence epilepsy.
source: However, tiagabine can also induce continuous SWDs (i.e. absence status epilepticus) in patients with absence epilepsy (Knake et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior clinical research.

claim: Tiagabine can induce non-convulsive status epilepticus in patients with focal epilepsy.
source: However, tiagabine can also induce continuous SWDs (i.e. absence status epilepticus) in patients with absence epilepsy (Knake et al., 1999) and non-convulsive status epilepticus in patients with focal epilepsy (Ettinger et al., 1999; Vinton et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: GAT1 knockout mice exhibit increased incidence of spike-wave discharges.
source: GAT1 knockout mice, which have increased inhibitory currents, and presumed increased activation of GABAB receptors (Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010) in thalamocortical neurons, also exhibit increased incidence of SWDs (Cope et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Application of GABAB receptor antagonists increases seizures in rats susceptible to convulsive focal seizures, but suppresses seizures in rats with non-convulsive absence seizures.
source: Furthermore, application of GABAB receptor antagonists increases seizures in rats susceptible to convulsive focal seizures, but suppresses seizures in rats with non-convulsive absence seizures (Vergnes et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Systemic injection of GABAB receptor agonists increases spike-wave discharges in animal models.
source: Specifically, systemic injection of GABAB receptor agonists increases SWDs (Liu et al., 1992; Bortolato et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Injection of GABAB receptor antagonists reduces or even abolishes spike-wave discharges in animal models.
source: Specifically, systemic injection of GABAB receptor agonists increases SWDs (Liu et al., 1992; Bortolato et al., 2010), while injection of GABAB receptor antagonists reduces or even abolishes SWDs (Liu et al., 1992; Vergnes et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The expression of the CaV3.1 T channel subtype by thalamocortical neurons correlates with spike-wave discharge expression in both animal models and human patients.
source: The expression of the CaV3.1 T channel subtype by thalamocortical neurons correlates with SWD expression in both animal models (Kim et al., 2001; Broicher et al., 2008; Ernst et al., 2009) and human patients (Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Blocking T channels reduces both thalamocortical neuron bursting and oscillations in thalamic slice models.
source: Blocking T channels reduces both thalamocortical neuron bursting and oscillations in thalamic slice models (Huguenard and Prince, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The average electrotonic length across all recorded neurons was 0.71 ± 0.08 space constants.
source: Notably, the average electrotonic length across all recorded neurons was 0.71 ± 0.08 space constants (range: 0.1-1.5 space constants), mitigating voltage attenuation concerns that might arise from applying currents through the soma with dynamic clamp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: A combination of high inhibition amplitude and fast inhibition kinetics is necessary for LTS production.
source: We conclude that a combination of high inhibition amplitude and fast inhibition kinetics is necessary for LTS production.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from computational modeling results.

claim: High inhibition amplitude causes sufficient T channel recovery, which appears to be necessary for the open probability discrepancy curve to reach an inflection point.
source: A high inhibition amplitude causes sufficient T channel recovery, which appears to be necessary for the open probability discrepancy curve to reach an inflection point [criterion (1) above].
evidence: This claim is based on inference from computational modeling results.

claim: Fast inhibition kinetics causes rapid depolarization during IPSC decay, which appears to be necessary for the slope of the open probability discrepancy curve to be high at the inflection point.
source: Fast inhibition kinetics causes rapid depolarization during IPSC decay, which appears to be necessary for the slope of the open probability discrepancy curve to be high at the inflection point [criterion (2) above], eventually driving the open probability discrepancy past LTS threshold.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from computational modeling results.

claim: Dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade eliminates thalamic oscillations by promoting sustained, GABAB receptor-mediated inhibition that promotes a convergence of instantaneous and steady-state T channel open probabilities.
source: Collectively, the results of these manipulations (Figure 7B, Video 3 and Video 4) support the hypothesis that dual GAT1+GAT3 blockade eliminates thalamic oscillations by promoting sustained, GABAB receptor-mediated inhibition that, in turn, promotes a convergence of instantaneous and steady-state T channel open probabilities, a condition that results in LTS failure.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from computational modeling results.

claim: Oscillations were evoked at intervals producing no rundown (once per minute).
source: We evoked oscillations at intervals producing no rundown (once per minute, Jacobsen et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research establishing the experimental protocol.

claim: Sprague-Dawley rats of postnatal day 11 to 17 (P11-P17), of either sex, were used in oscillation experiments.
source: Sprague-Dawley rats [Charles River Laboratories (RRID:RGD_734476), Wilmington, MA] of postnatal day 11 to 17 (P11-P17), of either sex, were used in oscillation experiments
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Male Sprague-Dawley rats of postnatal day 11 to 15 (P11-P15) were used in dynamic clamp experiments.
source: Male Sprague-Dawley rats of postnatal day 11 to 15 (P11-P15) were used in dynamic clamp experiments
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The 1.4-fold and 2-fold increase in oscillation duration corresponds roughly to the reported 1.5-fold and 2.2-fold increase in GABAB IPSC amplitude produced by GAT1 or GAT3 blockade, respectively.
source: That is, the 1.4-fold and 2-fold increase in oscillation duration corresponds roughly to the reported 1.5-fold and 2.2-fold increase in GABAB IPSC amplitude produced by GAT1 or GAT3 blockade, respectively (Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference comparing current experimental results with prior research.

claim: GAT3 blockade significantly prolonged oscillation period, while the effect for GAT1 blockade was modest, consistent with reported effects on isolated GABAB IPSC decay.
source: Additionally, GAT3 blockade significantly prolonged oscillation period, while the effect for GAT1 blockade was modest, consistent with reported effects on isolated GABAB IPSC decay (Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on inference comparing current experimental results with prior research.

claim: In each two-cell network, each successive oscillation cycle was initiated by a thalamocortical neuron rebound burst.
source: Finally, in our two-cell model thalamic network, each successive oscillation cycle was initiated by a thalamocortical neuron rebound burst (Figure 8C), similar to what has been reported in experiments when a reticular thalamic neuron and a thalamocortical neuron were simultaneously recorded during a thalamic oscillation (Bal et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 8C and compared to prior experimental research.
